outcome: The generalized repunit-prime infinitude conjecture remains unproven for every base b; the only developments since 26 January 2024 are (a) a computational primality *certification* (not a new discovery) of the base-10 probable prime R(109297), completed 26 May 2025 by Andreas Enge using elliptic curve primality proving (ECPP), and (b) continued discovery of larger base-10 probable repunit primes (e.g. R(8177207), found by Ryan Propper in 2021 and still listed as a probable prime as of 2025). Neither result bears on whether infinitely many repunit primes exist in any base.
credited_humans: Harvey Dubner (original 2007 discovery of the probable prime)
summary: This bullet asks whether, for any base b that is not a perfect power and not of the form -4k^4, there are infinitely many base-b repunit primes (the generalized repunit/Wagstaff-type conjecture). This is a classic 'infinitely many X' question, which under §3.1 moves only when actually answered — not when a new example is found or a probable prime is upgraded to a proven prime. I confirmed via the current Repunit Wikipedia article, the Prime Pages (t5k.org) top-20 repunit list, and the specific record page for R(109297) that: the conjecture is still completely open in the literature (no proof or disproof for any base, including base 10); the sole event dated within the window is the 26 May 2025 ECPP primality certificate for R(109297) (a probable prime originally found by Harvey Dubner in 2007), computed by Andreas Enge over roughly 20 months on a 64-core machine — a certified, non-AI, deterministic-algorithm computation, and in any case only a proof that one specific number is prime, not a step toward the infinitude question. I also confirmed R(8177207), the largest known base-10 repunit probable prime (found 2021, still unproven as of 2025), has had no status change. Searches for any AI involvement in repunit-prime work (LLM-driven number theory searches, AI-assisted primality proofs) turned up general AI-and-mathematics stories (Erdős problems, OEIS conjectures, Theo-Conjecture) but nothing whatsoever connecting AI systems to repunit or generalized-repunit primes. I also noted, but did not open or rely on, a GitHub repository ('vibemathing/problem-wikipedia-...') that surfaced in search results and appears to be another research pass on this same dataset; per instructions I did not read it and it played no role in this record. Status is therefore open, no_change_found true, matching and confirming the triage's 'none' verdict.
competing_reading: One could argue the ECPP certification of R(109297) deserves a `progress` classification as 'an instructive incident' of computational number theory, since it is a genuine new fact (a probable prime became a proven prime) dated within the window. But per §3.1, the bullet's question is existence of infinitely many primes, and a single case moving from probable to proven does not narrow or answer that question, so I classified it as `open` with `no_change_found` rather than `progress`. If the harness's convention is that any dated, sourced computational event on the topic should be surfaced as `progress` even when it doesn't bear on the infinitude question, this record would instead be `progress` / `ai_role none` / `resolution_direction null`.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of infinitude of repunit primes for even a single qualifying base b would settle this bullet as resolved/partial; short of that, only a change in expert consensus or a new heuristic/proof-adjacent result (e.g., a proof of infinitude conditional on a major conjecture like GRH) would move the status away from open. No such result was found.
